summary:
CrewPulse is an offline-first crew health monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It gathers key health indicators (resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, stress, mood, SpO2 and radiation dose rate) and helps astronauts evaluate and act on their own health status.

It addresses the challenge in three ways. First, every astronaut is compared with their own personal baseline, learned for each hour of the day, rather than a population average. Second, every alert is explainable: it states what changed, why it matters, and a suggested action. Third, it works fully offline, with no internet, backend or API keys, which fits the communication delays and outages of deep space.

The mission context shapes the alerts, covering solar particle events, sleep disruption, isolation fatigue and reduced exercise. The app is built with React, TypeScript, IndexedDB and a PWA service worker, with 141 automated tests.

All crew data is simulated, and every threshold is documented as an assumption. CrewPulse is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does and how it works
CrewPulse is an offline-first health monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long-duration missions. It tracks resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, stress, mood, SpO2 and radiation dose rate. It compares each astronaut with their own personal baseline, learned separately for every hour of the day so normal daily rhythms don’t trigger false alarms. When a deviation lasts several hours, CrewPulse raises one alert per episode. Every alert states what changed, why it matters, and a suggested action.

Benefits and intended impact
On long missions, communication delays and outages mean astronauts can’t always wait for ground support. CrewPulse lets them evaluate and act on their own health status. Because alerts are personal and explained, crew members can understand them and trust them, and alert fatigue is reduced.

Tools and technology
React, TypeScript (strict mode), Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Dexie (IndexedDB) and a PWA service worker. A seeded simulator generates reproducible crew data, including a solar particle event, sleep disruption, isolation fatigue and skipped exercise. The project has 141 automated tests. There is no backend, no API keys and no network dependency, so it works fully offline.

Creativity
Instead of fixed population thresholds, CrewPulse uses robust per-person, per-hour baselines (medians), so an early event in the baseline window doesn’t hide the next one. A type-level check makes it impossible to create an alert without all three explanation parts.

Factors we considered
Radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed environment shaped the indicators and scenarios. We also considered accessibility: status never relies on color alone, there is full keyboard navigation, and the layout works on phone and laptop.

Honesty and limits
All crew data is simulated. Every threshold is an assumption documented in docs/ASSUMPTIONS.md and needs checking against NASA sources. CrewPulse is a prototype and not a medical device.

We used Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, as a coding assistant to help plan the project, write and refactor code, write tests, and draft documentation. Our team reviewed, ran and tested the output, chose the challenge and the design principles, and made the final decisions. No generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers. All crew data is simulated and labelled as such in the app.
